title: Databases, subject headings and citation chaining
note: Scholarly databases add subject headings: a controlled vocabulary that tags each record by what it is about, whatever words the author used. PubMed's vocabulary is MeSH. Once you find one strong article, chain backward through its references and forward through the works that cite it.

read.title: Two ways to find what words miss
text: Keyword searching has a blind spot. One author writes "heart attack," another "myocardial infarction," a third "acute coronary event." A keyword search catches only the words you typed.

Subject headings close that gap. In MEDLINE, each article is tagged with terms from MeSH, the National Library of Medicine's controlled vocabulary. MeSH is a hierarchy: broad headings branch into narrower ones. When you search a MeSH term in PubMed, the search explodes by default, so it also retrieves articles tagged with the narrower terms beneath it. PubMed also tries to map your plain words to MeSH automatically, which is why a simple search often finds more than the words you typed.

The second technique is citation chaining. When you find one excellent article, its reference list points backward to the earlier work it built on. A tool like Google Scholar's "Cited by" link points forward to newer work that cited it, which shows how the conversation developed and whether later studies confirmed or challenged it.
Used together, these methods turn one good find into a network of related sources, and they reach studies that your first keywords never matched.
